article_text:
Carine Barret sent us her latest series shot in Cambodia. She writes:

A major community fishing event brings the village of Bangkoang, in Prasat Bakong District, Siem Reap Province, Cambodia, to life.

Rooted in an age-old tradition of the communities of Angkor, this festival takes place in March every year, on the eve of the ceremony marking the end of the rice harvest season.

In keeping with tradition, the fishing day takes place in an ancient reservoir and precedes spiritual rites dedicated to local guardian spirits. In rural Khmer tradition, the lake is regarded as a living space. Elders pay tribute to the spirits who protect it, while villagers pray for protection, abundant harvests and plentiful fish.

This fishing event is about more than providing food. It is considered an ancestral heritage of the Angkor region. The economy of the Khmer Empire relied on reservoirs and water basins, and some collective fishing traditions may date back to this ancient system of water management.

The event strengthens local identity, social bonds and collective memory.

Originally, only villagers were allowed to take part in the opening of the ceremony. Over time, the event has grown in popularity, and people from neighbouring communities now join in. Thousands of participants gather for this major annual occasion.

Everyone enters the muddy water together. The lake will be protected throughout the rest of the year, allowing fish to reproduce.

Traditional Khmer fishing methods are used, and the entire village takes part. Elders pass down traditional techniques, while children learn by watching.

Local regulations prohibit competition and individual fishing before the official start. There is no commercial purpose. The catch is shared fairly among the families.

The event is celebrated as a living cultural heritage of the Angkor region.

Once the fishing is over, it is time to share the catch and enjoy a meal together. Some of the fish are grilled on the spot over barbecues, while the rest is shared with relatives and taken home.

Food stalls are set up early in the morning. Communal meals spring up around the lake. Coming after the agricultural season, the event is also an opportunity for many families to reunite.

Carine Barret

Surprise! US Pavilion Needs More Cash to Ship Works Home

Commissioner Jenni Parido sent a letter to donors pleading for "urgent funding" for deinstallation and shipping as the Venice Biennale comes to an end.

Call Me the Breeze at the 2026 Venice Biennale (photo Hrag Vartanian/

Hyperallergic )

With less than a month left until the 61st Venice Biennale closes on November 22, the United States pavilion commissioner Jenni Parido has pleaded for additional donations to ship Alma Allen's sculptures out of Italy.

This week, the New York Times reviewed a letter by Parido, who founded the American Arts Conservancy (AAC) and commissioned Allen's exhibition in Venice. She told potential donors that the Trump administration-aligned arts nonprofit was “facing an urgent funding need associated with the final deinstallation and safe return of the artworks to the United States.”

The time-sensitive fundraising effort falls in line with Parido's financial model for this year's Biennale presentation. After months of opacity surrounding the selection process and funding ventures for the pavilion, Parido told Hyperallergic in April that Allen's exhibition, Call Me the Breeze , received no “corporate or foundation funding,” and that it was facilitated through the “generous support of private citizens who believe in the importance of American artists and cultural exchange.” The AAC also had an online donations portal to help fund the pavilion ahead of the Biennale's opening in May.

Hyperallergic )

article_text:
Barbara Jakobson was a monumental force in the New York art world for over 60 years, serving as an influential collector, a fierce patron, and a longtime trustee of New York’s Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). She also had a sharp, curatorial eye and a truly singular style. That is perhaps best evident in her home on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, which doubled as her own ever-evolving gallery from the mid-1960s until her death in 2025 . “I see the house as a vessel for an ongoing autobiographical exercise,” Jakobson told Curbed in a 2021 interview. “I keep the transformation as proof of life.”

The five-story townhouse along East 74th Street in the Lenox Hill neighborhood was built in 1910 and later expanded by architect John Kingsland in 1956. Prior to Jakobson, filmmaker Elia Kazan lived in the 20-foot-wide abode while directing East of Eden (1955) and Splendor in the Grass (1961). Hollywood stars including James Dean, Natalie Wood, and Marlon Brando reportedly visited then.

Jakobson, a native New Yorker, bought the pad in 1965 and lived there for nearly six decades. During that time, she welcomed New York’s creative set, such as artists Jasper Johns, Andy Warhol, Cy Twombly, and Robert Rauschenberg. After her death last summer, the property was brought to market in April 2026 for $9.8 million. It received a price cut of over $800,000 before reaching its current asking price of $8.99 million. Leslie Hirsch, Edward Joseph, Howard Morrel, and Benjamin Anderson of Christie’s International Real Estate New York hold the listing . Nicknamed “the Squirrel House” on account of the bronze squirrel sculptures at the entrance, the home is whimsical yet refined. Red lacquered doors open to 6,000 square feet of stylish interiors, with eight bedrooms and six full bathrooms spread throughout. A grand entry hall with triple arches and custom wallpaper by artist Peter Halley leads to a parlor floor featuring a formal living room, a gallery, and a salon with a wood-burning fireplace. A staircase—on which Jakobson was photographed for Vogue —spirals down to a spectacular double-height great room, where an outline of Frank Stella’s 1971 Felsztyn III remains. It once hung there but was sold in 2005 at a Christie’s auction featuring works from Jakobson’s collection. Glass doors lead out to a private 350-square-foot garden. The guest bedrooms, including two junior suites with dressing rooms and en suites, sprawl across the next two levels. The primary suite, meanwhile, covers the entire top floor, offering a light-filled private lounge for reading, relaxing, or even pondering art.

In celebration of Criterion’s The Complete Kubrick , we’re publishing a season of features dedicated to the filmmaker’s oeuvre and beyond, going through Criterion’s box set era by era and disc by disc—plus a couple of surprises from the archives. Explore more here and read part one below.

Early documentary shorts: Day of the Fight (1951), Flying Padre (1951), The Seafarers (1953)

While they, with one exception, bear little obvious resemblance to his later narrative features, the young Kubrick’s early shorts vividly illustrate qualities that made him a hotshot photographer at Look magazine. Exhibiting a quietly confident mastery of expressive angles and shot composition, each of these shorts evokes a whole milieu to contextualize their human-interest stories about intensely driven men.

In Day of the Fight , filmed in Kubrick’s native Manhattan, misty high-rises share visual space with cluttered streets and brick facades as middleweight boxer brothers Walter and Vincent Cartier, both WWII veterans, strive to punch their way to the top. They don’t just eat, train, and sleep together; they receive holy communion before a fight in a church scene shot with imposing Gothic awe by Kubrick “in case something should happen.” As in his Look career, Kubrick felt no obligation to be a neutral observer, introducing props and staged scenes or shots whenever he felt they would benefit the narrative: he lent his own dog to Walter to appear extra gentle while Douglas Edwards’ melodramatic narration describes his aggressive fighting style. Kubrick’s fascination with duality and irony, needless to say, was set from day one. His striking dramatic shots of boxers in the ring, meanwhile, would be heavily revisited (in some cases remade) for Killer’s Kiss .

Flying Padre , set in the sun-bleached hills and blazing clear skies of rural New Mexico, follows a lone Catholic priest tending to his topographically sprawling parish by light aircraft trips crisscrossing the county. On top of his first major onscreen engagement with Christianity, the film also happens to be the closest look at how a Kubrick-directed Western might have played: evocative wide shots of mule-riders on the road, expressionistic close-ups of sorrow-sunken faces and tilted wooden crosses in the tiny earthen graveyard of a small “Spanish-American” settlement.

The Seafarers , an educational film produced on commission for the Seafarers’ International Union , was only ever intended for a narrow audience. Those not looking to join the SIU may be less-than-enthralled by a half-hour explanation of their facilities and member benefits, and taking a shot every time Don Hollenbeck’s droning narration intones the word “seafarers” could prove fatal to many viewers. Yet the 1953 film is a fantastically preserved time capsule from the golden years of the American union, and morsels of Stanley Kubrick are still discernible in the director’s first color feature: pale-blue and beige-dressed men are dwarfed by stark, commanding technological structures and flat sheets of luminous color, at sea and in their industrial command center. Inside that command center, we see another fixation of Kubrick’s: a keen interest in the bawdy poster-girl pin-ups that decorate the men’s quarters and union barber shop, presented with frank amusement as the first sexually charged images in a Kubrick film.

Fear and Desire (1952)

“Boring and pretentious” were the blunt descriptors assigned to Stanley Kubrick’s narrative-feature debut by no less than an older and wiser Stanley Kubrick. Made at 23 with financing largely provided by his pharmacist uncle Martin Perveler, Fear and Desire is also the only film Kubrick would try to erase from his record, destroying what reels he could find and forbidding his wife Christiane from ever seeing it.

Sitting through it, the reasons for such extreme embarrassment become self-evident: the feature debut by one of history’s greatest filmmakers turns out to be a laughable amateur hour, 63 crawling and barely coherent minutes of Kubrick’s Greenwich Village actor friends doddering about the wooded mountains of SoCal like they’re filming The Blair Witch Project in WWII cosplay. Fear and Desire’s four physically and spiritually lost army men—played by Frank Silvera, Kenneth Harp, Paul Mazursky and Stephen Coit—break into near-constant monologuing, woodenly intoning such overcooked undergrad poetry as, “We spend our lives running our fingers down the lists and directories, looking for our real names, our permanent addresses.” (Kubrick would later recall this line with particular embarrassment.) The director’s first stab at fiction filmmaking also, somehow, comes across as a step backwards from his earlier documentary work: fewer subtle shots and cuts conveying its story of men pushed to the limit, more awkwardly edited action scenes, rambling voiceover, and performances flopping back and forth from scenery-chewing to anemic.

It’s actually kind of inspiring how bad Fear and Desire is, and in a way that comes out best in this complete Kubrick collection. Juxtaposed with his later masterpieces, Kubrick’s debut singlehandedly shatters the image of the boy genius preternaturally destined for greatness. Starting his career with a certifiable dog did not stop this fiendishly driven, hardworking, constructively self-critical filmmaker from becoming the Stanley Kubrick of legend. Even in its incompetence, Fear and Desire hints at motifs and fixations that would permeate for nearly half a century. It’s telling, for instance, that his very first war film was not a recreation of any specific historical conflict, but an abstract allegorical one in which neither side is identified by flag or ideology. Kubrick’s martial men are already finding that the real war is in themselves—not just the internal conflict with their own apelike tendencies, visualized by the film’s most shocking sequence of a hysterical soldier assaulting a female captive from a nearby village (Virginia Leith), but also absurdly literalized by the same men playing both armies. Kubrick’s fascinations with absurdism, duality, and the mask of civilization slipping are present, however inarticulately, right from ground zero.

Killer’s Kiss (1955)

Kubrick’s first “real” narrative film (or at least the first one he acknowledged) was still a rough-and-tumble independent production. While it doesn’t quite hold together on its own merits, it has decidedly more going for it than Fear and Desire , and gives much stronger indication of Kubrick’s tremendous visual gifts. Borrowing scenario elements (even entire shots) from Day of the Fight, the bare-bones noir caper follows a down-and-out boxer, played by Jamie Smith (seemingly unintentionally) as having taken a few too many blows to the head when he falls for a local gangster’s girl (Irene Kane, underutilized as the film’s most dynamic performer, in thrall to the returning Frank Silvera).

The script is still written by Howard Sackler (later to be known for The Great White Hope , years after his last collaboration with Kubrick) and its hammy dialogue and turgid voiceovers aren’t much improved. But there’s considerably fewer of them. Experimenting with nonverbal storytelling in a way he wouldn’t fully revisit until 2001: A Space Odyssey , the Kubrick of Killer’s Kiss instead leveraged the strengths he’d developed in photojournalism to fashion a stregnth that none of his more famous, immaculately polished films shot on epic London soundstages would ever replicate: extensive New York location photography vividly capturing the grit and local flavor of the midcentury streets he knew well. Combining his intimate feel for the city with the stark visual motifs of noir, Kubrick delights in shooting busy streets filled with dancers, pickpockets, and passersby, dusty windswept corners, windows seen through windows, billboards shining in the night, bright kitschy storefronts, and menacing alleyways where shadow-cloaked men wait, the dirt-flecked pavement and fog-smothered skyscrapers and claustrophobic interiors between them. Using the moody high-contrast aesthetics of the genre as a springboard—rest assured Killer’s Kiss does some remarkable things with lighting—Kubrick further juxtaposes New York City’s clean, angular Art Deco aesthetics and its dirty, messy underbelly both visually and thematically, furthering his career-long motif of beautiful modern structures concealing dark and nasty secrets.

While the narrative never really takes off before abruptly self-terminating in a hokey happy ending, it does lead to two especially striking sequences suggestive of later triumphs. Kane’s femme fatale Gloria gets one memorable, extended monologue detailing the tragic story of her ballet-dancer sister, delivered over a hauntingly composed sequence of Kubrick’s then-girlfriend, real-life ballerina Ruth Sobotka, twirling and bending gracefully on a darkened empty stage. And the film climaxes in a dreamlike chase filmed in eerily empty wide shots across alleys and rooftops, culminating in a showdown between murderous romantic rivals Smith and Silvera in a storage room packed with feminine mannequins. One only wishes Killer’s Kiss could do more to earn these subconscious-scraping images across a sub-70-minute runtime that, despite its many seductive sights, never quite finds a flowing rhythm or shape. As a visual storyteller, the young Kubrick of Killer’s Kiss is all the way there; it’s all those pesky words he can’t let go of but can’t quite get to work for him. With many of his subsequent films being literary adaptations made in partnership with top-shelf writers of the page and screen, Kubrick would never suffer this problem again.

article_text:
Un ritratto mediceo, una natura morta di rara eleganza, una versione della Monna Lisa e paesaggi italiani osservati attraverso lo sguardo di artisti europei. È un catalogo che intreccia scuole, epoche e sensibilità quello della prossima asta di Old Masters di Lempertz, in programma a Colonia il 21 novembre. In totale 277 opere, con una selezione che spazia dal Rinascimento al Barocco fino al vedutismo ottocentesco – e con un’attenzione particolare, come sempre, alla pittura italiana.

Tra i lotti di maggiore interesse figura il Cesto di vimini con pesche e gelsomini di Fede Galizia (80.000-100.000 euro), esempio della sua capacità di coniugare la tradizione lombarda con una rappresentazione minuziosa degli oggetti. La composizione, essenziale ed elegante, affida alla luce il compito di far emergere frutti e fiori dall’oscurità dello sfondo, valorizzandone ogni dettaglio.

Al Rinascimento ferrarese appartiene la Madonna col Bambino incoronati insieme a San Nicola da Tolentino e San Sebastiano (60.000-70.000 euro), un tempo attribuita a Lorenzo Costa e oggi ricondotta al Maestro della Maddalena Assunta, artista anonimo descritto da Roberto Longhi in L’officina ferrarese come interprete delle influenze di Costa e del Perugino. Di ambito fiorentino è invece il Ritratto di Alessandro de’ Medici, duca di Firenze di Carlo Portelli (20.000-25.000 euro), versione successiva del celebre dipinto di Giorgio Vasari. L’armatura, il sedile circolare e il drappo rosso assumono un preciso valore simbolico, alludendo rispettivamente alle imprese del duca, alla durata del suo regno e al sangue versato durante la rivolta contro i Medici.

Il catalogo comprende anche una copia della celebre Monna Lisa di Leonardo (12.000-15.000 euro), proveniente dalla Lyversberg Collection, e un San Giovanni Battista nel deserto attribuito alla scuola dei Carracci (10.000-15.000 euro). Di Giovanni Domenico Tiepolo è invece il disegno Ercole e Anteo (8.000-10.000 euro), parte di una serie di studi sul soggetto appartenenti alla fase avanzata dell’artista.

Tra le altre presenze di rilievo, due allegorie inedite di Antonio Bellucci: Il trionfo di Galatea (Allegoria dell’acqua) e Venere e Cupido (Allegoria delle arti) , entrambe stimate 25.000-35.000 euro. Pittore veneziano tra i più importanti tra Sei e Settecento, Bellucci sviluppò una carriera internazionale che lo portò anche a Vienna, dove tra il 1702 e il 1704 lavorò per il principe Johann Adam Andreas I del Liechtenstein.

Una sezione significativa da Lempertz è dedicata ai paesaggi italiani dipinti da artisti stranieri. Spicca il Lago di Bientina di Jacob Philipp Hackert (70.000-90.000 euro), realizzato dopo il suo trasferimento a Firenze, con una veduta catturata da Montecarlo, nei pressi di Lucca. Di Jean-Baptiste Lallemand è il Paesaggio con rovine (18.000-22.000 euro), composizione ispirata al Foro Romano e ai monumenti dell’antichità.

Da Lempertz , Venezia è protagonista delle Due vedute (San Giorgio Maggiore e Cannaregio con Palazzo Labia) di Friedrich Nery (20.000-25.000 euro), mentre Oswald Achenbach firma Davanti al Colosseo (con vista sulla fontana di Meta Sudans) (10.000-14.000 euro), dove il monumento romano è inserito in una scena animata da viaggiatori e commercianti. Completano la selezione due vedute veneziane di Carlo Grubacs: Veduta di Piazza San Marco (10.000-12.000 euro) e Veduta della Piazzetta di San Marco (6.000-7.000 euro).

Il percorso si conclude con altri scorci della penisola: dal Capriccio di Ippolito Caffi (2.500-3.000 euro) a Capo Miseno con vista su Ischia e Procida di William Bridge (3.000-4.000 euro), dalla Vista delle scogliere di Capri di Karl Theodor Boehme (5.000-6.000 euro) al Pescatore sul Golfo di Napoli di Albert Flamm (4.000-5.000 euro), fino al Paesaggio dei Monti Albani con vista su Castel Gandolfo di Franz Knebel (3.000-4.000 euro). Una selezione che restituisce la varietà dei soggetti e degli sguardi attraverso cui, tra Settecento e Ottocento, l’Italia emerge da protagonista.

article_text:
Doris Salcedo is best known for her moving “anti-monuments,” gigantic artworks—or sometimes negative spaces—that propose new ways to commemorate atrocities. Always, she focuses on the victims’ perspectives. Her best-known work, Shibboleth (2007), installed in Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, comprised one giant, scar-like crack in the concrete, rerouting foot traffic in a manner that evoked the jarring disruption of borders more broadly.

The Colombian artist began working at such a monumental scale only after she began losing her central vision. At age 31, Salcedo was diagnosed with Stargardt disease, a rare genetic condition, and today she is legally blind, with only peripheral sight.

Before her vision started to change, Salcedo made all her sculptures alone. Reflecting on that time during a visit to one of her studios in Bogotá in July, she remembered treasuring “the privacy of improvising and of working directly with the materiality.” But as her condition progressed, she had to give up solitude “little by little” and started working with assistants.

Naturally, she mourned surrendering the spontaneity her independence enabled. At first, Salcedo, now 67, found that “it was a very difficult adjustment, especially losing the privacy.” She also found that she had to “think in a different manner,” since “before, I was improvising; I never had a prior drawing.” When she works with a team, she has to come up with a plan she can clearly communicate: “Things have to be absolutely defined,” she explained. Slowly, though, she found that working collaboratively “gave me the possibility of making better pieces than the ones I was making by myself. A collective statement is far more powerful than a lonely solo voice. It becomes like a chorus, and a really potent one.”

In November, at White Cube Gallery in New York, Salcedo will premiere a sculpture that is the culmination of decades of this collaborative way of working—and huge in a way that could never be accomplished by one person. A full-sized house—at nearly 30 feet—has been woven entirely from human hair. When I visited, dozens of assistants were working across her three studios, tying knots in individual strands, a painstaking process. The resulting pattern resembles chicken wire or a chain-link fence.

Even working with such a big team, the process took three years. “To be thankful is not enough,” Salcedo said of the collective effort, adding that it could have easily taken 20 years to make on her own—and that she couldn’t spare that kind of time at her age.

As Salcedo led me through her studio—her own iconic salt-and-pepper curls rhyming with the looping locks lining the space—she told me that all of her workspaces were designed by the architect Carlos Granada. The two have been working together for 25 years. He is also the architect behind Fragmentos , Salcedo’s 2018 “anti-monument” commissioned by her national government to commemorate the 2016 Colombian peace agreement. Visiting the building in the heart of Bogotá, what at first looks like a typical modernist, single-floor gallery takes on new weight in the feel of its flooring: The textured tiling is made from firearms that once belonged to the Colombian guerrilla group FARC and were later melted down. Visitors walk right on top of these instruments of violence and fear, on tiles Salcedo made in close collaboration with 20 Colombian women who survived sexual violence during the conflict.

The work has an undeniably chilling effect. School groups flock to it regularly. Some critics, though, have found its message misleading, since several splinter factions are still active and thousands of fighters rejected that 2016 agreement. But for Salcedo, Fragmentos is not a static space: She regularly invites other artists whose work resonates to exhibit within its walls. When I visited, a crew was de-installing a sound installation by Hajrah Waheed that filled the space with movingly hummed songs of resistance. The work, titled Hum II (2023), is surprisingly affecting, unifying: You’re made to feel something of the song’s sentiments even if they’re in languages you don’t understand. Fittingly, the title means “we” in Urdu, Waheed’s mother tongue.

Like Fragmentos , Salcedo’s studios boast high ceilings. Her workspaces also feature glass brick walls and floating staircases: These are sparse spaces that enable her and her team to see what they are working on. As she walked me through, magnifying glass in hand, she pointed out that one of her studios is the same shape as the home she is building—a triangle atop a square, as if a kid drew a house. Eventually, we came upon the net-like hair arranged in sections like a gradient, growing darker and denser at the bottom. She let me touch it, and I was surprised to find it so sturdy and lightweight at the same time.

THE WORK-IN-PROGRESS MARRIED a complicated process to a simple shape. As we spoke, I found myself wondering about the latter—why a house? I found a hint in two books sitting on the surface of her desk, both of them scanned so she can see them on a screen in large print: Domicide: The Global Destruction of Home and Dreamhouse: Stories of Art and Shelter .

House is not her first work on the subject of the devastating effects of the global housing crisis. Uprooted (2020–22), her prize-winning work in the 15th Sharjah Biennial (where, as it happens, she met Waheed, a fellow prize winner), repurposed 804 dead trees into a mesmerizing, if uninhabitable, home. At almost 1,000 feet long, the work is meant to speak to the predicament of climate refugees. Her newer work, which takes the same shape, is about more deliberate displacement: specifically, “domicide,” which the authors of one of the books on her desk, J. Douglas Porteous and Sandra E. Smith, describe as the calculated destruction of homes. Explaining the impetus for her piece, Salcedo pointed to current conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, Syria, and Sudan, where people are being violently displaced en masse.

Domicide, she pointed out, has a cascading effect: victims lose not just a structure but their communities. They lose access to privacy and respite, as well as bathrooms and places to cook and sleep. Mental health, studies show, tends to deteriorate rapidly as victims are forced into survival mode.

With House , Salcedo wanted to show that, while the dispossessed are of course vulnerable, they are also resilient. Her meshy nets are fragile and flexible, yet they are also much stronger than they seem. Hair may be ephemeral, but she makes it structural and sturdy. It’s all inspired, she told me, by the ways that spiders make webs of silk, material they take from their own bodies. Pairing hair and home, she evokes the ways that bodies and buildings—like dignity and domesticity—are tightly bound.

SALCEDO LEARNED TO WORK WITH human hair from earlier pieces: “Unland” (1995–98) comprises tables severed and then rearranged such that they depend on dissimilar tables for structural support. As if personifying the balancing act, the artist intricately threaded the surfaces with hair, drilling tiny holes in the tables to insert locks she gathered from a local salon. But for House , given its magnitude, she decided to source hair online, learning to look carefully for certain certificates, as there is a lot of violent crime in the human hair trade.

Hair is not the only tricky material that will feature in her fall show. On an upper floor of one of her studios, more assistants were at work on objects of a smaller scale, all destined for display alongside House at White Cube. They were wearing jeweler’s glasses and using X-Acto knives to meticulously remove the starch from individual grains of rice. A team of architects and engineers looked on, huddled around a computer on a lofted level as they worked out the structure of the sculpture’s shape. “I’ve never had such a large team,” she explained as I took in the scene. At one point, she tried working with a renowned engineer who eventually stepped down, saying the idea was too complicated.

When an artist uses sculpture’s most stalwart materials like wood or bronze—as Salcedo has in the past—“the tools are already designed for you,” she said. House required more trial and error than she’s ever needed before—so it also required her biggest team yet. “I had to fabricate new tools and new ways of working,” she explained as we watched assistants drill minuscule holes in starchless rice grains before passing them along to the next station, where still other assistants would thread individual hairs through those tiny openings. They were assembling a kind of mesh, then forming it around damaged cooking supplies—bowls and pots and pans—to form Grains of Sorrow (2023–26), a reminder of what is lost to domicide besides simple structure.

If this sounds like an incredibly elaborate—and surprisingly elegant—way to speak to tragedy, for Salcedo, both beauty and labor are part of her point. She is cognizant of how her studio might provide jobs to those who need them, employing, for instance, 150 women from the Colombian countryside, where it is difficult for them to find work.

The decision to both scale-up and work elaborately is as conceptual as it is material: “My work has always been labor-intensive because in the Global South, labor is intensive,” she said. “It’s completely different from industrialized countries.” She meant this not only as a way to shine a light on contemporary conditions, but also as a retort to art-historical tropes: Modernity is too often narrated, she said, as if “no single person from the Global South participated. But we know all the labor and all the suffering created modernity.” She wants to combine the forms and traditions of European sculpture with painstaking labor to show the two were always intertwined.

I asked her about the role beauty plays for her; she replied that she’s received a lot of criticism on this matter. She maintained, however, that “in all the violence and terror I’ve been researching all my life, I think the abject part belongs to the perpetrator,” adding that “beauty has a lot to do with dignity”—something she wants to restore as she tells the stories of victims. Elegance is also a way to get people to really look: The stories she’s telling are almost always in the newspapers, but that doesn’t mean everyone stops to soak them in. Salcedo doesn’t want you to divert your eyes from the world’s horrors, so she goes to extreme lengths to make sure you can’t look away.

article_text:
Pulse-pounding psychological horror game “ Madison ” is going to splash some blood on the silver screen.

L.A.-based Story Kitchen , a production company specializing in game-to-movie adaptations, has inked a pact with “Madison” developer Bloodious Games to develop a feature film set in the world of the first-person horror title.

Currently, there’s no casting info for the “Madison” movie or other details on the production including expected release date, director or screenwriter. The project does not yet have a distribution partner but Story Kitchen is targeting it for a theatrical release.

Related Stories

Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal

In the “Madison” game, you play as Luca Maxwell, who has received an instant camera as a 16th birthday present. Unfortunately for Luca, the camera is inhabited by a demon that forces him to continue a murderous ritual started decades ago by a satanist serial killer (the titular Madison). Players must solve puzzles using the camera to try to break the cycle of madness.

Popular on Variety

Story Kitchen, co-founded by “Sonic the Hedgehog” movie franchise producer Dmitiri Johnson, is spearheading several other game adaptations. Those include the “Tomb Raider: The Legend of Lara Croft” animated series for Netflix, “Life Is Strange” (Prime Video) and “Streets of Rage” (Lionsgate) .

First launched in 2022, “Madison” has received multiple awards and recognitions, including best narrative – grand winner at the NYX Game Awards and best game at EVA 2022. Bloodius also has released an immersive VR version of the game.

The partnership with Story Kitchen comes as Bloodious continues to expand the “Madison” universe. The Maxwells’ Curse, a new story expansion, is set to arrive in 2027, free for all “Madison” owners. In addition, a free Halloween update to the game introduces two difficulty modes: an expanded Normal Mode, designed to make the experience more accessible to newcomers to horror and puzzle games; and Possession Mode, an “intense new challenge that pushes even the most experienced players to their limits.”

“’Madison’ earned its reputation one heartbeat at a time. Players don’t just remember the story; they remember what it did to them,” Story Kitchen co-founders Dmitri Johnson and Mike Goldberg said. “Our job is to carry that physical experience into a theater without losing what makes it Bloodious’s world.”

Bloodious founder Alexis Di Stefano, the game’s creator and director, said, “We built ‘Madison’ to be felt, not just played. Story Kitchen understood from the first conversation that the camera, the house, the Maxwell family, and the terrifying entities behind it all aren’t just set dressing; they’re the franchise. That’s who we wanted to build the next chapter with.”

Story Kitchen has a TV first-look deal at Amazon MGM Studios and an animated film first-look deal at DreamWorks Animation. The company is repped by WME and Pryor Cashman.

article_text:
知性の歴史から生成AIを問う

「KYOTO EXPERIMENT 2026」 で上演されたホー・ルイアンのレクチャー・パフォーマンス『歴史のすがた／知能の立脚点』（2024年初演）は、一枚の画像をめぐる問いから始まる。

2016年、ホーはGoogle Cultural Instituteで、シンガポールの画家チュア・ミアティーによる《Epic Poem of Malaya》（1955）の人物像が、顔照合アプリによって別の顔写真と結びつけられる場面を目にした（＊1）。画像を照合し、分類するAI（人工知能）は、そこに描かれた人物の歴史的な意味までとらえているのだろうか。この経験を起点に、本作は、生成AIが過去の資料から学習し、新たなイメージを生み出すことの意味を、知性の歴史から問い直す。

舞台の中央にホーが座り、その左右にふたつのスクリーンが並ぶ。左側にはレクチャーに関連する映像や資料が映し出され、右側には前半、ホーの発話をリアルタイムで文字に変換したテキストが表示される。ドキュメンタリー映画のナレーションのように流暢なホーの語りを、文字は少し遅れて追いかける。後半になると、右側のスクリーンには、ホーが入力した言葉をもとにAIが生成した画像が映し出される。

歴史を学習する機械

ホーがたどるのは、AIの技術史だけではない。シンガポールの植民地史から、国家による社会の計画・管理、現代の「スマート・ネーション」構想に至る歴史を通じて、情報によって社会を把握しようとする知性のあり方を描き出す。また、マーシャル・マクルーハンの「グローバル・ヴィレッジ」という構想を手がかりに、世界をネットワークとしてとらえる発想と情報技術の発展との結びつきをたどる。こうして本作は、生成AIを、社会や世界を認識し、管理しようとする歴史的な構想の延長線上に位置づける。

生成AIは、大量の画像やテキストからパターンを学び、新たな出力を生み出す。しかし、学習データは世界を均等に記録したものではない。何が記録・保存され、知識として利用されるかは、歴史的な条件に左右される。画像が生成AIの学習データとして再利用されても、そこに刻まれた権力関係が消えるわけではない。資料が生まれた背景や文脈が捨象され、過去のパターンだけが新たな出力のために再編されうる。

ホーが参照する映画『オール・ユー・ニード・イズ・キル』（2014）では、主人公が同じ一日を繰り返しながら戦闘の経験を積み重ね、時間が巻き戻っても記憶や技能を次のループへと持ち越していく。いっぽう、周囲の状況はリセットされ、経験の蓄積と、それを生み出した出来事とが切り離される。この時間のループは、AIの仕組みにも通じる。学習によって情報の規則性が抽出されても、その情報が生まれた文脈までが引き継がれるわけではない。過去から何かを学ぶことと、その背景を理解することのあいだには隔たりがある。

身体の形態と動作の知識

『歴史のすがた／知能の立脚点』では、画像生成AIが身体を描く際に、指の本数や手足のかたちが不自然になる例も取り上げられる。AIは、学習データに含まれる身体の画像からかたちや配置のパターンを学び、新たなイメージを生成する。しかし、身体の形態を画像として再現することと、身体を動かすなかで働く知識とは異なる。身体を動かすには、感覚を手がかりに動作を調整し、その結果を確かめながら、姿勢や力の加減を身につけていく必要がある。

AIがこうした能力を今後どこまで獲得できるかは、あらかじめ限定できない。ここで問題となるのは、AIに身体があるかないかということではなく、画像から抽出されたパターンが、対象のどのような側面をとらえ、何をとらえきれないのかという点である。身体を動かす経験を通じて得られる知識に目を向けることは、知性を情報の処理や形態の再現だけではとらえきれないことを考える手がかりとなる。

レクチャーと画像生成の時間

後半では、ホーは自ら生成AIを操作して画像を生成し、続いて、上演前に観客から集めたプロンプトを入力していく（＊2）。ランダムに選ばれたメモのひとつからは、メラニア・トランプとイーロン・マスクが踊る画像が現れた。ホーが緻密に構成したレクチャーに、観客の言葉をもとに生成された画像が差し込まれる。生成結果への反応や、ときに交えられる冗談を通じて、あらかじめ構想された語りに、その場で生まれるやりとりが重なっていく。

観客の言葉は画像生成のきっかけとなるが、出力は必ずしも意図どおりにはならない。入力された言葉から想像されるイメージとは異なる画像や、不自然な表現が現れることもある。こうした言葉と画像とのずれは、入力と出力のあいだにある不確定性を示すと同時に、言葉が画像へと変換される過程で、何が保持され、何が変化するのかという問題を浮かび上がらせる。

本作では、情報が別の形式へと変換される際に要する時間も観客の目の前に示される。ホーの発話は少し遅れて文字になり、プロンプトから生成される画像は、輪郭の曖昧な状態から徐々に鮮明になっていく。前者では語りが文字として記録されるまでの時間差が、後者では言葉が画像へと変わる過程が可視化される。情報が処理され、出力されるまでの時間もまた、上演を構成する要素となっている。

歴史を解釈し直すレクチャーと、言葉から画像を生成する実演。本作は、このふたつの時間を並置し、技術の歴史を意味づける営みと、技術が作動するプロセスとを交差させる。技術の現在を、その成立の経緯や歴史的文脈に照らして理解することは、技術の作動そのものから自ずと導かれるわけではない。本作は、この隔たりを解説するのではなく、異なる時間をひとつの上演のなかに重ねることで、技術を歴史的に理解することの条件を考えさせる。

＊2──ホーは、本作の2024年の初演以降、より写実的な画像を生成できるAIモデルへの更新を行わなかった。技術の性能を示すこと自体を目的とした作品ではないためだと説明している。

何をもって知性とみなすのか

本作が浮かび上がらせるのは、情報を処理し、一定のパターンを再現することを、どこまで理解と呼べるのかという問題である。歴史を理解することは、過去の情報を集めるだけでなく、それがどのような状況のもとで生まれ、誰によって、どのような観点から伝えられてきたのかをたどることでもある。

AIの知性を人間の知性と比較するだけでは、この問題はとらえきれない。情報を整理し、規則性を見いだし、対象を再現することは、AIだけでなく、人間が知識を形成し、世界を理解しようとする営みにも通じている。本作は、AIが理解しているかどうかを問うにとどまらず、私たち自身が何をもって理解と呼び、知性とみなしているのか、その前提を問い直す。

Source: A24

‘You Can See Everything’

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything stormed to a number two debut at the North American box office on a confirmed $15.6m through A24, delivering the biggest documentary debut in more than two decades since Fahrenheit 9/11.

The feature has been one of the major talking points within awards circles since its surprise screening at Telluride last month and sees HBO star Fielder embed inside the rental home of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in 2023 before she reports to prison after being found guilty of defrauding investors in her biotech start-up.

The R-rated You Can See Everything opened on 855 screens and scored the biggest debut by a film on less than 1,000 since Borat in 2006, and will expand next weekend. Grossing $5.5m on Friday, $5.2m on Saturday, and $4.8m on Sunday, it was a big hit with the Gen Z and Millennial crowd, with 70% of the audience was aged under 35 and a 55%-45% male-female split. The film scored all-time-high 4.8 score on Letterboxd, 99% on Rotten Tomatoes.

This weekend’s performance will only intensify speculation over whether the film will become the first documentary to earn a best picture Oscar nomination. The story of Holmes clearly has enduring appeal. Amanda Seyfried starred in Hulu’s 2022 limited series The Dropout . The entrepreneur’s 11-year sentence was reduced due to good behaviour and she is scheduled for release in 2030.

Paramount secured its first post-merger number one as the video game adaptation Street Fighter opened top of the charts on $31m from 3,575, while two other debuts filled out the top five. 20th Century Studios’ well-reviewed underwater thriller Whalefall directed by Brian Duffield and starring Austin Abrams from Resident Evil arrived via Disney in fourth place on $8m from 3,065.

America’s largest maximum-security prison, long notorious for its reliance on solitary confinement, Angola runs on the forgotten."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gary Tyler, a fiber artist and activist, remembers Angola. He arrived in 1974 at seventeen years old, wrongly convicted of shooting a white student during a segregationist mob’s attack on his school bus. The prison is bound on three sides by bayou, bluffs, and swamp; escaping into one’s mind was easier. His grandmother was a quilter, he said, and fabric could be found or bartered. Time was given. Over four decades inside, including two stints on death row, he got good, even renowned. Craftswomen from across the South came to Angola to find the man behind the textiles making rounds outside."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“All that time, I never thought of myself as an ‘artist,’” Tyler said at the opening of “Rebirth,” a solo show of his quilted and appliquéd works at the Grand Rapids Art Museum . “I said, ‘Call me a hobbyist.’ Artists were people in galleries, people with an audience.”", "links": [{"text": "Grand Rapids Art Museum", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/grand-rapids-art-museum/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Gary-Tyler-Rebirth-GRAM-Installation-2.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of “Gary Tyler: Rebirth” at the Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan. Courtesy the Grand Rapids Art Museum", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Rebirth” is one of three solo presentations on view in Grand Rapids through January 2027 that showcase art by or about people once incarcerated within the United States. An overflowing bucket of Kentucky Fried Chicken, lobster, steak, burgers and fries, pecan pie. Nothing, sometimes: inmates can refuse or be denied a selection. The Defense Secretary called for the military’s first execution in six decades—by firing squad—to be livestreamed. The White House launched an online arcade, where in one game a pixelated Border Patrol agent, rounds up “border crossers.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The art can’t hope to match the volume of cruelty. article_text:
Louisiana State Penitentiary, known as “Angola” for the slave plantation that once occupied its land, lies at the dead end of Highway 66.

Past the gate, the road continues—invitation permitting—through 18,000 acres of penal farmland punctuated by gun towers, barbed-wire enclosures, and incarcerated men picking crops on the so-called farm line. America’s largest maximum-security prison, long notorious for its reliance on solitary confinement, Angola runs on the forgotten.

Gary Tyler, a fiber artist and activist, remembers Angola. He arrived in 1974 at seventeen years old, wrongly convicted of shooting a white student during a segregationist mob’s attack on his school bus. The prison is bound on three sides by bayou, bluffs, and swamp; escaping into one’s mind was easier. His grandmother was a quilter, he said, and fabric could be found or bartered. Time was given. Over four decades inside, including two stints on death row, he got good, even renowned. Craftswomen from across the South came to Angola to find the man behind the textiles making rounds outside.

“All that time, I never thought of myself as an ‘artist,’” Tyler said at the opening of “Rebirth,” a solo show of his quilted and appliquéd works at the Grand Rapids Art Museum . “I said, ‘Call me a hobbyist.’ Artists were people in galleries, people with an audience.”

“Rebirth” is one of three solo presentations on view in Grand Rapids through January 2027 that showcase art by or about people once incarcerated within the United States. Ray Materson, whose show is subtitled “Metamorphosis,” works in a medium he invented during his prison sentence for a drug-fueled robbery with a toy gun: palm-sized embroideries stitched by hand from the threads of unraveled socks, Americana meets Renaissance miniature.

The third show is The Last Supper , a 1,000-piece ceramic installation by the artist Julie Green, shown in its entirety for only the second time. For twenty years, up until their death in 2021, Green illustrated final-meal choices on ceramic plates painted in cobalt blue and re-fired in her kiln. What does the condemned order on death row? An overflowing bucket of Kentucky Fried Chicken, lobster, steak, burgers and fries, pecan pie. Nothing, sometimes: inmates can refuse or be denied a selection. (Final meal selections are generally a matter of public records.) At a quick glance, these plates might pass for Staffordshire. A closer look could ruin your lunch.

“It’s not so much that these shows are timely,” said Jennifer Wcisel, curator of collections at the Grand Rapids Art Museum. “It’s that the question of what incarceration means to American life is never absent. It’s ongoing.”

But has punishment been so openly advertised since the pre-Civil Rights era? Tennessee’s botched attempt to execute Christa Pike, the only woman on its death row, was followed by a magazine interview with the physician on hand to pronounce her dead (he said the state should try again). The Defense Secretary called for the military’s first execution in six decades—by firing squad—to be livestreamed. The White House launched an online arcade, where in one game a pixelated Border Patrol agent, rounds up “border crossers.”

The art can’t hope to match the volume of cruelty. It aspires to empathy or at least empathy’s catalyst: curiosity. Whose aim does a public execution serve? Within the carceral system, how is dignity doled out?

The Last Supper argues that dignity is a fickle allowance. Texas ended special last meals in 2011, after white supremacist Lawrence Russell Brewer ordered a feast and left it untouched. Set against Green’s terrible, tender plates, the result is hard to defend. Bite-size biographies like “he never had a birthday cake so we ordered a birth-day cake for him” give way to row upon row of “Standard prison fare.” This is dinnerware for a haunted house.

It is also a map of America’s patchwork principles on capital punishment. The Supreme Court barred executing people with intellectual disabilities in 2002, then left the states to define who qualifies, within limits. One plate records an IQ of 61, well below the benchmark of about 70, and a request that the menu not be released to the media. Another records a request that their meal be saved until after the execution.

Everything on view is portraiture, if the word can stretch to cover a spirit given a recognizable shape, even one abridged to a birthday cake. Tyler and Materson work with representational directness in the opposite register from Green. We see faces. Their work can indulge fantasy, the province of the living. One of Tyler’s quilts depicts a former inmate known as Big Toe in the so-called Greek Alps, still wearing the armor from The Life of Jesus Christ , a play produced by the drama club Tyler founded. Portraiture at its best is said to reveal the heart. For centuries it was also a privilege of the powerful, who commissioned likenesses to control how they were seen. Prison inverts that arrangement: the powerful do the watching. But what does surveillance ever capture of its subjects? Insight can’t be taken, only given.

Materson’s intricate embroideries stray in their subjects from baseball to outer space, with the most striking blending imagination and documentation. In Self-Portrait (undated), he sits before a mirror, stitching the very piece the viewer is looking at. Down a receding tunnel, a smaller Materson stitches a smaller Materson, and so on: infinity, or its likeness. The thick black frame that cages his face is made of the same thread as the rest, not impossibly undone.

One quilt late in Tyler’s show features a great crane, the kind that roosted in the wetlands around Angola and sometimes landed in the prison yard. Tyler was released in 2016, after decades of campaigning by activists including Rosa Parks. The crane captures that moment. His soul, he said, sprang skyward on his first step outside. It has yet to descend.

Others at Angola have hard landings.

Tyler’s Convict Poker (2025) unfolds at the Angola prison rodeo: a Black man hangs in midair, bucked from a bull. The last of its kind in the country, the event is held twice a year and open to a paying public. Spectators can’t legally bet; the gamble belongs to the prisoners who volunteer. In convict poker, a raging bull is loosed on a mock card game, and the last man still seated wins a prize. Posting this October’s rodeo to Facebook, an attendee wrote: “The announcer said they didn’t run that fast from the PoPo 🚓😂 Watch til the end, prisoners were flying…”

Tyler never rode in the rodeo. But he doesn’t judge. (One of his quilts were raffled at the rodeo and raised $30,000 for the hospice program.) The men who volunteer, he said, are willing “to jeopardize their lives or go through a sense of degradation just to entertain an audience because nobody wants to be forgotten.”

“These are men who may never go home. The announcer mentions their names, and that they are serving life sentences; understand?”

Brazil’s Maeve Jinkings, renowned for her pivotal role in Walter Salles’ Oscar-winning “I’m Still Here, ” joins the cast in the upcoming prison convent escape drama “Cabildo 71,” which is selected to participate in Ventana Sur ’s Proyecta Co-Production Forum.

Jinkings is also best known for her roles in “ The Secret Agent” director Kleber Mendonça Filho’ s lauded dramas “Neighboring Sounds” and “Aquarius.”

Una Presencia (Argentina) and Vitrine Filmes (Brazil/Spain) have come on board as co-producers of the project, which is backed by Argentina’s INCAA minority fund and the Ancine–ACAU bilateral minority fund. They join lead producer Monarca Films of Uruguay and co-producer Boulevard Filmes, Brazil.

Written and directed by Victoria “Pitoka” Pena, whose debut feature, “Delia”, won the Silver Biznaga for Best Director at the Málaga Film Festival, “Cabildo 71” is based on real-life events about the women imprisoned in Cabildo — a prison-convent run by the nuns of the Good Shepherd, which included Lucía Topolansky, who later became the VP of Uruguay and wife of former President José “Pepe” Mujica, her twin sister Elia Topolansky and other women who became prominent figures in Uruguay’s political and social life.

Story follows La Parda who joins forces with 12 political prisoners to form a women’s choir, using it as a cover to escape from the Cabildo prison-convent. During Mass on March 8, 1970, they rush down the chapel aisle and escape right under the noses of the nuns guarding them.

A year later, La Parda is captured again. This time, there are no nuns—only police and a growing number of prisoners, including her sister, Lucía. The two barely speak, but La Parda senses that Lucía is hiding something.

Behind the prison walls, a daring plan is taking shape: the biggest women’s prison escape in history.

“I am interested in telling this story from an intimate and personal point of view, giving this dimension precedence over the heroic narrative of the feat. Without diminishing what was achieved — quite the opposite — I want to delve into the issues that shaped the prisoners’ lives within the intimacy of the prison: the differences among them that give substance to their experience, in order to explore identity, betrayal and the need to find one’s own sense of justice,” said Pena.

Said Monarca Film’s Eugenia Olascuaga: “We want to portray the female characters within their variety of social class and the kind of life they led, not under the “guerrilla women” stereotype that the popular imagination tends to default to.” “The eight Uruguayan actresses who will play the Tupamaras are confirmed — it was very important for us that they all be Uruguayan, as a political and artistic choice.”

She added that the actresses playing the Topolansky sisters are Graciela Ingold and Carolina Genoni while the rest of the cast are Camila Parard, Renata Denevi, Luche Bolten and Matilde Colacce. Jinkings plays one of the nuns in the convent-prison.

Principal photography is slated for Sept. to Nov. next year.

Ventana Sur takes place in Montevideo, Uruguay over Nov. 30 – Dec. 4.

レストランから消えたピカソの版画6点、衣類と工具箱の下から発見。約1カ月ぶりに無傷で戻る

南仏のレストランから盗まれた ピカソ の版画6点が、約1カ月後に無傷で回収された。隠し場所は、アパートの一室に積まれた衣類や工具箱の下。容疑者7人が逮捕され、関係者に安堵が広がった。

フランス 南部のコート・ダジュールで盗まれた パブロ・ピカソ （1881-1973）の版画6点が、約1カ月後にアパートの一室から無傷で回収された。作品は、積み重なった衣類や工具箱の下に隠されていたという。

版画が盗まれたのは、ムージャンにある老舗レストラン「ラマンディエ（L’Amandier）」だ。フランス料理の巨匠ロジェ・ヴェルジェが1977年に開いた店で、過去にはミシュランの星も獲得している。ムージャンは、ピカソが1961年から1973年に亡くなるまで暮らした村としても知られる。

10月2日午前2時ごろ、手袋と覆面を着けた男2人が店内に侵入し、1分足らずで版画を持ち去った。その朝、オーナーのマチュー・オータンが盗難に気づき、地元当局に通報。国家憲兵隊のカンヌ捜査班が捜査を担当した。

ベルギーのメディア、 ラ・リーブル によると、被害額は10万ユーロ（約1780万円）を超えると推定される。ピカソ作品としては比較的低い金額だが、売却は容易ではなかったようだ。

カンヌの国家憲兵隊を指揮するギヨーム・プレディ中佐は、フランス紙 ル・モンド に対し、盗まれた版画は「簡単に売りさばける作品ではなかった」と説明した。容疑者たちは美術市場に精通しておらず、買い手を見つけるための知識や人脈も持ち合わせていなかったという。むしろ、「薬物や武器に関する犯罪で知られる者たち」だった。とはいえ、捜査には迅速な対応が求められた。プレディは、その理由をこう語る。

「急いで動かなければなりませんでした。こうした作品は転売され、そのまま美術市場に戻ってこなくなる危険性が高いのです」

11月3日、国家憲兵隊員約40人がアパート2軒を捜索し、版画を発見。18〜30歳の容疑者7人が逮捕された。ル・モンドによると、窃盗の実行に関与した疑いのある3人と、共犯者4人だという。憲兵隊は、作品が完全な状態で回収され、返還されたと発表している。

この事件は被害額こそ比較的小さいものの、ヨーロッパで美術品盗難が相次ぐなかで注目を集めた。2025年に大きく報じられたルーブル美術館の 盗難事件 以降も、フランスのカーニュ＝シュル＝メールにある ルノワール美術館 や、イタリア・パルマ近郊の マニャーニ・ロッカ財団 などで作品が盗まれている。

今回の回収には地元の美術館関係者からも安堵の声が上がった。ムージャン女性芸術家美術館の館長、リーザ・パオリは、次のように喜びを語った。

「作品が戻ってきて、本当にうれしく思います。もう国外に持ち出されてしまったのではないかと考えていました」

一方、ラマンディエのオーナーであるオータンは、安堵する一方で、いささか困惑した様子も見せた。フランスのテレビ局フランス2（France 2）に、こう話している。

「防犯体制を見直す必要があるかもしれません」（翻訳：編集部）
